trial_name: PROTECTION — Perioperative IV Amino Acids for Kidney Protection in Cardiac Surgery (2024)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Landoni G, Monaco F, Ti LK, Baiardo Redaelli M, Bradic N, Comis M, et al. A randomized trial of intravenous amino acids for kidney protection. N Engl J Med. 2024;391:687-698.
trial_type: RCT — multinational, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group
one_liner: In adults undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery, a perioperative amino acid infusion reduced the incidence of AKI (26.9% vs 31.7%; RR 0.85) and stage 3 AKI (1.6% vs 3.0%; RR 0.56) compared to placebo, without affecting mortality or need for kidney-replacement therapy.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) scheduled for elective cardiac surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass, with an expected ICU stay of ≥1 night and a baseline creatinine available preoperatively.
pico.intervention: Blinded continuous IV infusion of a balanced amino acid mixture (Isopuramin 10%) at 2 g/kg ideal body weight/day (max 100 g/day), started at operating-room admission and continued for up to 72 hours, until ICU discharge, initiation of KRT, or death.
pico.comparison: Blinded continuous IV infusion of placebo (Ringer’s solution) at the same rate and with the same stopping rules.
pico.outcome: In-hospital AKI (KDIGO creatinine criteria, stage ≥1) within 7 days after surgery.

background.existing_knowledge: Cardiac surgery–associated acute kidney injury (AKI) is common and associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and subsequent chronic kidney disease.
background.knowledge_gap: Beyond supportive measures, proven preventive pharmacotherapy has been lacking.
background.hypothesis: Perioperative continuous intravenous infusion of a balanced amino acid mixture, intended to recruit renal functional reserve and increase renal perfusion, would reduce postoperative AKI compared with placebo.

methods.design: Investigator-initiated, multinational, multicentre (22 centres, 3 countries), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial.
methods.setting: Perioperative operating room and ICU setting in Italy, Singapore, and Croatia.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) scheduled for elective cardiac surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass
exclusion: Advanced chronic kidney disease (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2)

methods.intervention: Blinded continuous infusion of balanced amino acid mixture (Isopuramin 10%) at 2 g/kg ideal body weight/day (maximum 100 g/day), started at operating-room admission. Continued until 72 hours after initiation, ICU discharge, initiation of kidney-replacement therapy, or death (whichever occurred first). If enteral/parenteral nutrition started within 72 hours, infusion rate adjusted to target total amino acid intake of 2 g/kg/day.
methods.comparison: Blinded continuous infusion of placebo (Ringer’s solution) at the same rate and using the same stopping rules and adjustment approach.
methods.blinding: Double-blind: patients, clinicians, investigators, data collectors, and outcome assessors blinded; statisticians and authors blinded during analysis; pharmacists/trial nurses aware but not involved in data collection/analysis.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned n=3500 (1750/group) to detect a 20% relative risk reduction in AKI (assumed 25% in placebo) with 90% power at two-sided α=0.05, accounting for three interim analyses using O’Brien–Fleming boundaries.
methods.primary_outcome: In-hospital AKI (KDIGO creatinine criteria, stage ≥1) within 7 days after surgery.
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome assessed within 7 days; mortality at ICU/hospital discharge and at 30, 90, and 180 days; quality of life at 180 days.

headline_bullets: AKI occurred in 26.9% with amino acids vs 31.7% with placebo (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.77 to 0.94; P=0.002).
Severe AKI (stage 3) was lower with amino acids: 1.6% vs 3.0% (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87).
Patient-centred secondary outcomes (kidney-replacement therapy, length of stay, mortality) were similar between groups.

outcomes_table.outcome: In-hospital AKI (KDIGO creatinine criteria), within 7 days
outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome; 2 missing in amino acid group.
Event rates low; no clear between-group difference.
No mortality signal despite AKI reduction.
No ADRs reported in either group.

safety: No adverse drug reactions were reported in either group.
Surgical revision for bleeding: 4.0% vs 3.5% (RR 1.13; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.58; P=0.48).

domains.notes: Central, web-based randomisation with computer-generated permuted blocks, stratified by site; concealment maintained by central service.
Double-blind across clinicians/patients/outcome assessors; small numbers of unblinding by mistake (2 vs 2) reported.

One placebo-group patient withdrew consent before infusion initiation; otherwise near-complete follow-up for in-hospital outcomes. Primary ITT with prespecified imputation approaches and supportive per-protocol/as-treated analyses showing consistent direction of effect.

Major deviations were uncommon: study infusion never started (16 [0.9%] vs 17 [1.0%]); premature and permanent discontinuation of infusion (48 [2.7%] vs 56 [3.2%]). Crossover was rare (3 [0.2%] vs 1 [0.1%]).
Groups were closely matched (e.g., median age 66 vs 67 years; female 30.1% vs 30.1%; median preoperative creatinine 0.96 vs 0.94 mg/dL; hemofiltration during CPB 9.9% vs 9.2%).

internal_validity.verdict: Strong. Allocation concealment and blinding were robust, event ascertainment was objective, deviations/crossover were infrequent, and the intervention exposure was well matched except for amino acid content.

domains.notes: Adult elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass in high-income settings; predominantly White (98%+), with 30% women; centres largely Italian with small numbers in Singapore and Croatia.

Intervention is pragmatic (standard infusion product, bedside titration rules) and could be implemented where perioperative ICU infusion protocols exist; transferability to lower-resource settings is less certain given case-mix, baseline risk, and care pathways. Key exclusions: advanced CKD (eGFR <30) and patients already receiving/planned for KRT; results may not generalise to emergent cardiac surgery or off-pump pathways.

external_validity.verdict: Findings are highly applicable to elective on-pump cardiac surgery populations in high-income systems, but extrapolation to advanced CKD, emergency surgery, and settings with markedly different perioperative care infrastructure should be cautious.

strengths: Prespecified interim analyses and sensitivity analyses
limitations: AKI defined primarily by creatinine (limited urine-output data capture post catheter removal)
Management bundle adherence (e.g., avoidance of hypotension/nephrotoxins) not reported

critical_appraisal.summary: A large, well-conducted RCT demonstrating a reduction in creatinine-defined AKI with a pragmatic amino acid infusion, but the absence of effects on patient-centred outcomes and lack of injury biomarkers limit the clinical significance of the finding.
strengths: Robust double-blind, multicentre design with low protocol deviations and crossover
Objective, prespecified primary outcome with consistent results in sensitivity analyses
weaknesses: Reliance on creatinine-based AKI definition without urine output or biomarker confirmation
No demonstrated benefit on kidney-replacement therapy, length of stay, or mortality

sections.authors_conclusion: Perioperative amino acid infusion reduced creatinine-defined AKI and stage 3 AKI after elective cardiac surgery, without detectable safety trade-offs, but did not change kidney-replacement therapy, length of stay, or mortality.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: For centres seeking a pragmatic AKI-reduction strategy in elective on-pump cardiac surgery, amino acid infusion is a plausible option; whether it improves patient-centred outcomes or long-term kidney health remains uncertain.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery in high-income settings, excluding those with advanced CKD (eGFR <30).
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not prove the intervention prevents tubular injury or improves hard clinical outcomes like mortality or need for dialysis.
implementation_caveats: The reduction in AKI did not translate to reduced KRT, LOS, or mortality.
The mechanism may be functional (increased filtration) rather than structural protection.

controversies.notes: Absence of kidney injury biomarkers (e.g., NGAL, KIM-1) limits inference on whether the observed reduction in creatinine-defined AKI reflects true tubular protection or predominantly functional changes in filtration.

controversies.topic: Baseline creatinine ascertainment and AKI definition
controversies.notes: Concerns were raised that using preoperative creatinine values drawn from records (potentially up to 365 days before admission) could affect AKI classification; authors stated baseline creatinine was obtained in the week before surgery in all patients.

Criticism that the control fluid could differentially affect renal perfusion via chloride load was countered by authors noting low chloride concentration and low infusion rate, arguing physiological implausibility of chloride-driven effects.

Exclusion of eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and lack of proteinuria/albuminuria stratification were raised as limitations for broader kidney-risk phenotyping; authors argued concealed randomisation makes major baseline imbalances in such factors unlikely.

A 2024 perioperative meta-analysis (including cardiac surgery trials) reported reduced AKI with IV amino acids overall and suggested reduced hospital length of stay, supporting a class effect on perioperative AKI risk, while still leaving uncertainty about long-term kidney outcomes and patient-centred endpoints.
The trial’s methodological manuscript and prespecified analytical approach were published before completion, supporting interpretability and reducing analytic flexibility concerns.

unresolved_questions: Does the reduction in creatinine-defined AKI translate to improved long-term kidney function or reduced progression to CKD?
Would the benefit be replicated in a more diverse population, including those with advanced CKD or undergoing emergency surgery?
Is the mechanism functional (renal functional reserve recruitment) or structural (tubular protection)?
Can the addition of injury biomarkers clarify the clinical significance of the AKI reduction?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Perioperative amino acid infusion reduces creatinine-defined AKI after elective cardiac surgery, but with no proven benefit on dialysis or survival, its role is as a pragmatic, low-risk AKI-reduction strategy, not a practice-changing mandate.
